title: Turkish Airlines flight 634
summary: The Avro RJ100 crashed on final approach to Diyarbakır in thick fog conditions. The crew descended to 500 feet and below, well below the MDA of 2800 feet, despite poor visibility. The GPWS issued multiple alarms but the crew did not abort. The aircraft struck the ground 900 meters short of the runway threshold with a positive pitch angle.
probable_cause: The captain continued the descent below the MDA in thick fog conditions without visual references, continued to 500 feet and beyond with the GPWS alarming, and did not abort the approach in time.

The crew did not initiate go-around procedure immediately upon GPWS alarm but delayed before deciding to abort, then crashed 8 seconds later
The airplane struck the ground with the undersurface of the fuselage and the landing gear 900 m short of the runway threshold

title: Air Midwest 5481
summary: Flight 5481 pitched nose-up immediately after takeoff to 54° despite pilot inputs to descend. The stall-warning horn sounded and after reaching 1,150 ft, the aircraft stalled and descended uncontrollably, impacting an aircraft hangar 35 seconds after takeoff. Investigation found the elevator control cables had been incorrectly adjusted during recent maintenance by a mechanic unfamiliar with the aircraft type, and the post-adjustment test was skipped. Combined with the aircraft being overloaded from underestimated passenger weights, this resulted in insufficient elevator travel and pitch control authority.
probable_cause: The airplane was unable to descend after takeoff due to insufficient elevator control authority caused by incorrect cable adjustment during maintenance combined with the aircraft being overloaded and out of balance. The elevator control cables had been set incorrectly by a mechanic who had never worked on this aircraft type, and the post-flight control test that would have detected this deficiency was not performed.

title: Space Shuttle Columbia disaster
summary: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry on February 1, 2003, when a piece of insulating foam broke off from the external tank during launch and struck the thermal protection system tiles on the orbiter's left wing. The impact created a hole in the heat shield that went undetected during the mission. When Columbia re-entered the atmosphere, hot gases penetrated the damaged area, destroying the internal wing structure and causing the orbiter to become unstable and break apart over Texas and Louisiana, killing all seven astronauts.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by damage to Columbia's thermal protection system tiles on the left wing caused by foam insulation that broke off from the external tank during launch. The damage went undetected during the mission. During re-entry, hot atmospheric gases penetrated through the damaged heat shield and destroyed the internal wing structure, causing the orbiter to become aerodynamically unstable and break apart.

factors.evidence: The orbiter became unstable and broke apart during re-entry over Texas and Louisiana, with debris dispersing over a wide area.
A piece of insulating foam broke off from the Space Shuttle external tank during launch, a problem that had occurred during previous launches but the hazard was not adequately addressed.
Engineers at NASA did not initially notice the debris strike and could not determine the level of damage sustained because no camera had a clear view of the debris impact.

The certification and risk management process did not adequately address the known hazard of foam shedding from the external tank or assess the potential consequences of impact to the thermal protection system.
Similar foam shedding had occurred during previous Space Shuttle launches, causing damage ranging from minor to near-catastrophic, but the hazard was not resolved before the Columbia mission.

events.text: STS-107 launch initiated; Columbia orbiter with external tank and two solid rocket boosters.
During ascent, a piece of insulating foam broke off from the external tank and struck the thermal protection system tiles on the orbiter's left wing.
NASA Intercenter Photo Working Group did not notice the debris strike until the second day of the mission; no camera had clear view of impact.
Columbia re-entered the atmosphere over Texas and Louisiana after 16-day orbital mission; hot atmospheric gases penetrated the damaged heat shield area.
Orbiter disintegrated during re-entry as hot gases destroyed the internal wing structure, causing aerodynamic instability and breakup; all seven crew members killed.

notes: This is a space vehicle, not a conventional aircraft, but included in the batch.

Space Shuttle flight operations were suspended for more than two years after this disaster.
Debris Assessment Team dismissed Boeing's modeling predictions showing potential for deep damage, citing previous instances of predictions exceeding actual damage.
CAIB report (Columbia Accident Investigation Board) documented extensive investigation and organizational issues.

title: 2003 Iran Ilyushin Il-76 crash
operator: Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps
summary: On 19 February 2003, an IRGC Aerospace Force Ilyushin Il-76 carrying 275 people crashed into the Sirch mountains southeast of Kerman, Iran, while flying from Zahedan to Kerman in poor weather with strong winds; there were no survivors. Investigators concluded it was a controlled flight into terrain caused by deteriorating weather and high winds, though a militant group later claimed responsibility.

title: 2003 Congo air disaster
summary: On 8 May 2003, Ilyushin Il-76MD UR-UCB operated by Ukrainian Cargo Airways was conducting a charter flight from Kinshasa to Lubumbashi carrying soldiers and families, over 160 people crammed into the cargo compartment on benches and the floor. Approximately 45 minutes after takeoff at 10,000 feet, the cargo door suddenly opened causing explosive decompression. Many passengers were blown out of the aircraft while survivors described chaos with people screaming and clinging to ropes and netting. The aircraft managed to return to Kinshasa. The Congolese government confirmed 17 deaths while other estimates ranged much higher.
probable_cause: Cargo door opened in flight either due to improper fastening or failure after multiple closure attempts; investigation determined the door had been improperly fastened prior to takeoff or was opened by a passenger or computer glitch.

title: Colgan Air 9446
summary: Colgan Air Flight 9446 crashed into water near Yarmouth, Massachusetts shortly after taking off from Barnstable. The maintenance crew had improperly replaced the forward elevator trim cable and skipped a required step in the maintenance process. The maintenance manual depicted the trim drum backwards, causing the trim system to move opposite to pilot inputs. The flight crew did not perform the preflight checklist, which included an elevator trim check, allowing the dangerous misconfiguration to go undetected.
probable_cause: The maintenance crew's improper replacement of the forward elevator trim cable combined with an inadequate functional check of the maintenance performed, together with the flight crew's failure to follow the checklist procedures and the aircraft manufacturer's erroneous depiction of the elevator trim drum in the maintenance manual.

title: FedEx Express 647
summary: FedEx Express Flight 647, an MD-10-10F cargo aircraft carrying an experienced flight crew of two pilots plus five off-duty FedEx crew members, was scheduled to depart Oakland for Memphis at 08:10 CST on 18 December 2003. After a brief delay, the aircraft departed at 08:32 and the flight was uneventful until landing. The aircraft touched down on runway 36R at approximately 12:26 CST, and almost immediately the right landing gear collapsed. The aircraft veered off the right side of the runway and caught fire, but all seven occupants successfully evacuated.
probable_cause: The first officer did not properly line up the aircraft before touchdown, nor did she slow the aircraft adequately before touchdown, resulting in an excessively hard landing. During landing, a crosswind component caused the right wing to drop approximately six degrees, which was beyond the design capabilities of the right main landing gear, causing it to collapse. The captain failed to adequately monitor and check the first officer's work.
